Photograph: Sutton Liberal democrats Liberal Democrats Deselected candidate claims Lib Dems’ religious discrimination cost him £790,000 David Campanale seeks damages after what he says was organised campaign against his faith in Sutton and Cheam Aletha Adu Political correspondent Fri 21 Aug 2026 15.16 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 15.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google How much is a career in politics worth? The Liberal Democrats , despite admitting claims of religious discrimination, say about £22,800. A former Lib Dem candidate claims £790,000. It is a question before the Central London county court after David Campanale argued that discrimination against his Christianity cost him his political career in a civil case against the party. Campanale, a former BBC journalist, was selected in 2021 as the party’s candidate for Sutton and Cheam, but was removed in August 2023. The Liberal Democrats have admitted claims of direct and indirect discrimination on grounds of religion or belief under the Equality Act and their failure to deal with complaints Campanale made about his treatment, leaving the amount of damages to be determined by the court. Campanale’s schedule of loss, seen by the Guardian, puts his claim at £788,740.75, including interest. It seeks compensation for injury to feelings, aggravated damages, past and future earnings, the loss of an MP’s pension, counselling costs and the “loss of a chance”, or “loss of political capital”. But in a counter-schedule filed on Friday, the Lib Dems described Campanale’s claim as “grossly inflated and egregious”. Their lawyers say £14,000 should be awarded for injury to feelings, and as a volunteer political party member, Campanale could have been expected to withstand “rigorous political debate and criticism”. They put aggravated damages, past and future loss of earnings, an MP’s pension and the loss of political capital at £0. Campanale says he was mocked and abused over his Christian beliefs and faced an organised campaign to remove him, while some activists refused to campaign for him. In his claim Campanale said that at a meeting in January 2022, he was questioned about his Christianity by about 30 people and asked whether he was enjoying his “martyrdom just like Jesus did”. He also claims he was excluded from election leaflets and told not to campaign in certain wards because activists disagreed with his beliefs. His claim also referred to a phone call in March 2022 in which he said Luke Taylor, his replacement, told him that he had no right to a conscience based on his faith and that a “secular party” was being built with no place for Christians. After Campanale was removed, Taylor won the seat with a majority of 3,801. The seat has since become safer territory for the Lib Dems with recent polls putting them well ahead of the Conservatives. The case has prompted criticism from senior Liberal Democrat figures inside and outside the party. The former leader Tim Farron and former deputy leader Simon Hughes have backed calls for an independent inquiry. Farron has urged the party to apologise, saying there had been “manifest discrimination” against Campanale and party figures at all levels of the party failed to intervene. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Rowan Williams, the former archbishop of Canterbury, warned the position taken by the Liberal Democrats could make it “impossible” for Christians and people with other strong religious beliefs to represent the party. Before admitting the claims, the Lib Dems said in their defence that the party could deselect candidates where the expression of religious beliefs conflicted with its policies or values. The Lib Dems defence also described as a “statement of fact” the claim that the era associated with prominent Christian Liberal Democrats such as Shirley Williams and Charles Kennedy was over. A Lib Dem spokesperson said before their submitted counter-schedule: “This is an ongoing legal case so it would not be appropriate to comment. The Liberal Democrats are home to people of all faiths and none, including many Christians. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/tis.text: The Budapest Times Tisza picks academic with no law degree to lead corruption recovery office The National Assembly's Committee on Justice and Constitutional Affairs is nominating Anna Róza Unger, an associate professor at the Faculty of Social Sciences of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), to serve as president of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH). At the committee’s Thursday session, it also decided to nominate Katalin Tasnádi as deputy president for investigations, while declaring the tender for the position of deputy president for public finance matters unsuccessful following the candidate hearings. István Hantosi, the committee’s Tisza-affiliated chair, said at the opening of the session that the selection of the office’s officials is accompanied by enormous public expectation and responsibility, given that confronting the past is one of Tisza Párt’s most important commitments. According to estimates, some 30 to 60 thousand billion forints of public assets may have “migrated into private pockets” over the past two decades, an amount that could equal one full year’s worth of Hungary’s total national debt. For this reason, the party committed to establishing the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office in order to put a stop to corruption involving public funds, asset loss, and asset stripping, and to hold accountable those who managed and abused the public assets entrusted to them irresponsibly, he stressed. He added that the NVVH’s task will not be political score-settling, but rather the recovery of public funds and the uncovering of serious corruption cases. At the same time, by establishing the office, they hope not only to shed light on the past but also to lay the “foundations of a clean future,” said István Hantosi. At the doorstep press conference held after the session, István Hantosi said the decision had been extremely close, as they had heard exceptionally strong concepts and ideas during the hearings. Regarding the declaration of the deputy president for public finance position as unsuccessful, he said they would like to launch another round in order to provide as many professional candidates as possible with the opportunity to compete through a broader and deeper pool of applicants. When asked when the new calls for applications for the deputy president positions could be issued, he replied that they would not waste time and that this could happen in the near future. In response to the suggestion that the office would be starting its work without three deputy presidents, he said the organisation and operation of the NVVH is most comparable to that of the prosecutor’s office, and since a deputy president for investigations had been elected, the investigative phase that underpins the work would be secured. Anikó Hallerné Nagy (Tisza Párt), a member of the committee, praised Anna Róza Unger, who — in her view — had been extremely convincing and resolute, possesses “a sense of neutral mission in the best sense of the word,” and is a highly committed professional. Anna Róza Unger had a clear grasp of the organisational structure, had firm ideas, and “her personality and concept will be the guarantee that the organisation fulfils the function that was one of Tisza’s greatest commitments,” the politician said. In response to the suggestion that Anna Róza Unger lacks a legal qualification, he said that the candidate has a very serious research background and is a substantial theoretical expert, alongside whom the professional aspects will be embodied by the vice-presidents overseeing the relevant fields. He commented on Anna Róza Unger’s statement at her hearing — that a court ruling might not come even within six years — by saying that, starting from the general order of justice, “this may be realistic,” but that it does not mean results cannot be achieved through civil law instruments, and that partial results may also emerge. In response to a question, Anikó Hallerné Nagy said she considers it not a failure but a responsible decision that no result was announced for the three vice-presidential posts, and that further work is instead being invested in finding the best candidates. She stressed that the final vote result does not mean the other candidates were not suitable for the position. She also expressed her thanks for the assistance and support of civil organisations. The Fidesz members of the committee did not attend the session. Artificial intelligence was used for the translation of parts of the original Hungarian text. https://www.kalb.com/2026/09/23/new-law-.text: Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google RAPIDES PARISH, La. (KALB) - Local politicians and law enforcement officials celebrated the grand opening for a new Rapides Parish Sheriff’s Office substation on Highway 71 between Lecompte and Cheneyville on September 23. The groundbreaking occurred last January and the facility became operational in July. It will serve the Cheneyville, Lecompte, Echo and Poland communities. Rapides Parish Sheriff Mark Wood says this substation will be an added convenience for the communities it serves. " They can do all their one-stop shopping right here," says Wood. “Instead of having to go to Alexandria, they can come right here and talk to folks about their case. A detective will be here working with them. It’s something convenient for the people that’s a long ways from Alexandria.” The substation will have 24-hour dispatch, a detective and other law enforcement officials. “Rapides Parish is about the second, third largest land mass parish in the state,” says Wood. “It’s a lot of area right here to cover so this is something that’s been needed right here. We’ve been waiting on this.“ Like other substations in the parish the new substation will be combined with the local fire department, Rapides Fire District 12, making emergency services more easily available.
